title: THEY WERE FIGHTING BEFORE THEY WERE BORN… BUT GOD HAD ALREADY SPOKEN OVER THEIR FUTURE
paragraphs: THEY WERE FIGHTING BEFORE THEY WERE BORN… BUT GOD HAD ALREADY SPOKEN OVER THEIR FUTURE
Two brothers. One exhausted mother. A battle inside the womb. And a family scandal that would reveal something breathtaking about God's grace: your beginning does not have to determine your ending.
“And the children struggled together within her; and she said, If it be so, why am I thus? And she went to enquire of the LORD.” — Genesis 25:22 (KJV)
Imagine carrying two children beneath your heart, only to discover that the struggle between them had already begun before either one had taken his first breath.
Imagine praying for a miracle for twenty years, finally receiving the answer, and then finding yourself whispering a question you never expected to ask.
God, why does the blessing hurt this much?
That was Rebekah.
And perhaps, in a way you have never considered, that has been you.
Because there are seasons when the very thing you prayed for becomes the place where you struggle the most.
You prayed for a marriage, and now you are fighting to keep it alive.
You prayed for a family, and now you lie awake wondering how to bring everyone back together.
You prayed for an opportunity, and now the responsibility feels heavier than you imagined.
You prayed for God to change your life, but the process of change has exposed wounds you thought were already healed.
And somewhere between the promise and the pain, a frightening question begins to rise.
Lord, if You answered my prayer, why am I still struggling?
Genesis 25 takes us into a home where that question was more than a passing thought.
It was a mother's reality.

But what happened inside Rebekah's womb would become part of a much greater story—a story involving favoritism, deception, betrayal, separation, divine mercy, and a promise that would eventually lead us to Jesus Christ.
And the most astonishing part?
The God who knew these brothers before they were born would not abandon His purpose when their family became a scandal.
Stay with this story.
Because the struggle in the womb was only the beginning.
And the grace waiting at the end is greater than you might expect.
Isaac was forty years old when he married Rebekah.
He was the son of Abraham, the child through whom God had promised to continue His covenant purposes.
But there was a painful problem.
Rebekah could not conceive.
Scripture does not describe every conversation they had, every disappointment they endured, or every private tear they shed. We should not pretend to know what God has not revealed.
But Genesis gives us two details that make the weight of their waiting unmistakable.
Isaac married at forty.
And he was sixty when his sons were born.
Twenty years stood between those two moments.
Twenty years in which the promised family line had not yet produced the next generation.
Genesis 25:21 tells us:
“And Isaac intreated the LORD for his wife, because she was barren: and the LORD was intreated of him, and Rebekah his wife conceived.” (KJV)
The Hebrew describes Isaac's prayer with the verb וַיֶּעְתַּר (vayyeʿtar), from the root עתר (ʿ-t-r), associated here with earnest supplication.
Isaac pleaded with the Lord.
And the Lord answered.
Notice what the passage does not say.
It does not say Isaac manipulated God into giving him children.
It does not say his prayers earned a miracle.
It does not say that every faithful couple who prays will receive the same earthly answer.
It tells us that Isaac prayed, and in this particular covenant story, God graciously granted his request.
That distinction matters.
Because God's faithfulness is not measured by whether He gives every believer the same outcome.
His faithfulness rests in His character, His promises, and ultimately in Jesus Christ.
Some prayers are answered in ways we recognize immediately.
Others are answered differently from what we hoped.
And some longings remain painfully unresolved in this life.
But the absence of the outcome we desire is not proof that God has stopped listening.
Then came the pregnancy.
The long-awaited answer.
The miracle.
The future.
And suddenly, something was terribly unsettling.
“And the children struggled together within her…” — Genesis 25:22 (KJV)
The Hebrew is striking:
וַיִּתְרֹצֲצוּ הַבָּנִים בְּקִרְבָּהּ
Vayyitrotzatzu habbanim beqirbah.
“And the children struggled together within her.”
The unusual verb וַיִּתְרֹצֲצוּ (vayyitrotzatzu) comes from a Hebrew root associated with crushing or violent pressure. In this context, it describes intense struggling or jostling.
This was not presented as an ordinary, peaceful pregnancy.
Something was happening inside Rebekah that distressed her deeply enough to seek the Lord.
And her response was painfully human.
“If it be so, why am I thus?”
The Hebrew expression is compressed and difficult to reproduce word for word in natural English. Its sense conveys Rebekah's distress and bewilderment over what she was experiencing.
She did not yet know the full significance of the struggle.
She knew only that something was wrong.
So she went to inquire of the Lord.
That detail deserves our attention.
Rebekah did not receive a complete explanation before seeking God.
She sought God because she did not understand.
There is a difference between bringing our questions to God and allowing our questions to drive us away from Him.
Rebekah brought her confusion into His presence.
And the Lord answered with words that would shape generations.

“Two nations are in thy womb, and two manner of people shall be separated from thy bowels; and the one people shall be stronger than the other people; and the elder shall serve the younger.” — Genesis 25:23 (KJV)
Two nations.
Two peoples.
A struggle extending beyond the lives of two brothers.
And a startling reversal of the expected order.
The older would serve the younger.
In the ancient world, the firstborn son ordinarily held a position of special inheritance and family privilege.
But God declared that His covenant purpose would unfold through the younger son.
Before the twins had spoken a word, chosen a path, or performed a deed, God had announced His sovereign purpose.
This is not a story about God being surprised by human behavior.
It is a story about God accomplishing His purposes in a world filled with deeply flawed people.
But be careful here.
The passage does not give us permission to declare that every conflict in a family was personally arranged by God.
Nor does it teach that every painful circumstance is a secret prophecy of future greatness.
The revelation given to Rebekah concerned these particular children and the nations that would descend from them.
Its meaning is anchored in God's covenant dealings with Abraham's family.
Yet the story reveals a truth every believer desperately needs.
God's purposes are not defeated by human weakness.
And that becomes even clearer when the twins are born.
The first child emerged red and hairy.
They named him Esau.
The second came out holding his brother's heel.
They named him Jacob.
Genesis 25:26 says:
“And after that came his brother out, and his hand took hold on Esau's heel; and his name was called Jacob…” (KJV)
In Hebrew, Jacob's name is יַעֲקֹב (Yaʿaqov).
It is connected in the narrative with עָקֵב (ʿaqev), meaning “heel.”
Later, Esau uses a wordplay on Jacob's name when accusing him of taking what belonged to him (Genesis 27:36).
But Jacob's name should not simply be translated as “deceiver” in every context. The biblical narrative develops that association through Jacob's actions and the brothers' conflict.
And those actions would become painfully consequential.
Because the struggle that began before birth did not end in the delivery room.
It followed them into adulthood.
Esau became a skillful hunter, a man of the field.
Jacob became a quieter man, dwelling among the tents.
Their differences were not inherently sinful.
But their family began to divide around them.
“And Isaac loved Esau, because he did eat of his venison: but Rebekah loved Jacob.” — Genesis 25:28 (KJV)
Read that again.
Isaac loved Esau.
Rebekah loved Jacob.
The Bible does not hide the favoritism.
And anyone who has lived in a divided household knows how destructive favoritism can become.
One child feels chosen.
Another feels overlooked.
One parent defends what the other condemns.
And slowly, love becomes tangled with competition.
Perhaps you know what it feels like to be compared with a sibling.
Perhaps you grew up believing you had to achieve more, earn more, or become someone else before you would finally be enough.
Perhaps you were the favored one and only later understood the damage that favoritism caused.
Or perhaps you are a parent looking back at choices you wish you could change.
The Bible does not romanticize this family.
It shows us a household where the people carrying God's covenant promises were still capable of wounding one another.
And then came the bowl of stew.
Esau returned from the field exhausted and hungry.
Jacob was preparing food.
Esau wanted some.
Jacob demanded something extraordinary in return.
“Sell me this day thy birthright.” — Genesis 25:31 (KJV)
Esau agreed.
Genesis 25:34 ends with a devastating assessment:
“Thus Esau despised his birthright.”
He traded something of lasting significance for immediate satisfaction.
It is a sobering picture.
Not because hunger is sinful.
Not because physical needs are unimportant.
But because Esau treated his birthright as something disposable.
How often does temptation operate in a similar way?
It presents an immediate desire as though nothing else matters.
One more secret conversation.
One more dishonest decision.
One more compromise.
One more night of returning to something God has been calling us to leave behind.
And suddenly, what seemed small begins to reshape a life.
But Jacob was not innocent.
His willingness to exploit his brother's desperation exposed something troubling in his own heart.
One brother treated a sacred privilege lightly.
The other took advantage of the moment.
Neither gives us a model of godly character.
And the story grows darker.
Years later, when Isaac was old and his eyesight had failed, Rebekah helped Jacob deceive his father into giving him the blessing intended for Esau.
Jacob wore his brother's clothing.
He covered his skin to imitate Esau's hairiness.
He brought food to his father.
And he lied.
More than once.
He even invoked the name of the Lord while explaining how he had obtained the food so quickly (Genesis 27:20).
Imagine that.
A man connected to God's covenant promise using deception and religious language to secure what he wanted.
The Bible does not excuse it.
And neither should we.
God had already declared His purpose before the twins were born.
Jacob did not need to manufacture God's faithfulness through dishonesty.
Yet the family chose manipulation instead of trust.
And when Esau discovered what had happened, his grief was overwhelming.
Genesis 27:34 describes him crying out with a great and bitter cry.
Soon afterward, his anger became murderous.
He intended to kill Jacob after their father's death.
The brothers who had struggled in the womb were now divided by betrayal.
Jacob fled.
Rebekah lost the daily presence of the son she had tried to protect.
Esau carried bitterness.
Isaac's household was fractured.
And the promised family looked painfully unlike the peaceful picture we might expect.
This is where the story begins to reach into places many people keep hidden.
Because some families do not fall apart through one dramatic event.
Sometimes the fracture begins with years of small wounds.
An unfair comparison.
A secret resentment.
A parent who never apologized.
A sibling who never felt seen.
An inheritance dispute.
A betrayal that everyone knows about but no one wants to discuss.
Then one day, the family gathers around a table and realizes that the people sitting together have not truly been close for years.
And someone wonders whether anything broken that deeply can ever be restored.
Jacob's story does not offer a simplistic answer.
There were consequences.
There was distance.
There was fear.
There were years of uncertainty.
But there was also a God who had not abandoned His covenant.
On his journey away from home, Jacob stopped for the night and slept with a stone beneath his head.
He was far from the security of his family.
He had not earned a reputation for integrity.
He was running from the consequences of deception.
And there, in an unlikely place, God met him.
Jacob dreamed of a stairway reaching toward heaven, with angels ascending and descending.
And the Lord reaffirmed the covenant promise given to Abraham and Isaac.
Then came these words:
“And, behold, I am with thee, and will keep thee in all places whither thou goest…” — Genesis 28:15 (KJV)
Think about the timing.
God did not wait until Jacob had become a mature example of spiritual faithfulness before confirming His covenant commitment.
He met Jacob while his life was still deeply complicated.
That does not mean God approved of Jacob's deception.
Grace is not divine permission to continue sinning.
It means that God's covenant faithfulness was greater than Jacob's failure.
And that distinction changes everything.
Because some people believe their worst chapter has permanently disqualified them from ever drawing near to God.
They remember the marriage they damaged.
The trust they destroyed.
The addiction they concealed.
The money they mishandled.
The words they cannot take back.
The person they used to be.
And even after years have passed, they still hear an accusation in their minds.
You know what you did.
Yes.
God knows too.
But the Gospel does not begin with the claim that our sins are imaginary.
It begins with the truth that our sins are real—and that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
Jacob would still have to face painful lessons.
Years later, the deceiver himself would experience deception in Laban's household.
He would work, suffer, fear, and eventually face the prospect of meeting Esau again.
But before that reunion, something extraordinary happened.
One night, Jacob wrestled with a mysterious man until daybreak.
Genesis 32 reveals the encounter as a profound confrontation with God.
Jacob emerged wounded.
He also emerged with a new name.
Israel.
Genesis 32:28 says:
“Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed.” (KJV)
The Hebrew name יִשְׂרָאֵל (Yisraʾel) is explained in the passage through Jacob's striving with God and with men.
The precise linguistic derivation has been discussed by scholars, but the narrative meaning is clear: Jacob's identity was being marked by his encounter with God.
The man who had once grasped his brother's heel now clung to God for blessing.
He did not walk away untouched.
He limped.
And perhaps that detail is more meaningful than we realize.
Because sometimes the evidence that God has dealt deeply with a person is not that they emerge looking stronger than ever.
Sometimes they emerge humbler.
More dependent.
Less willing to trust their own cleverness.
More aware of their need for mercy.
Not every wound is a spiritual lesson sent by God, and suffering should never be romanticized.
But God can use even painful experiences to expose our pride and teach us to depend on Him.
Jacob's life was changing.
And then came the moment he had feared.
Esau was approaching.
The brother he had wronged.
The brother who had once intended to kill him.
Jacob prepared for danger.
He arranged his family.
He bowed as he approached.
He had no guarantee that Esau would receive him peacefully.
And then Genesis 33:4 gives us one of the most moving scenes in the Old Testament.
“And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept.” (KJV)
They wept.
Two brothers who had struggled before birth.
Two brothers divided by rivalry and deception.
Two brothers whose history contained bitterness, fear, and years of separation.
Now standing face to face.
Weeping.
There is no indication that every consequence of their past disappeared.
Their reunion did not erase the years they had lost.
And the text does not teach that every broken relationship will end with a safe or joyful embrace.
Some people must maintain boundaries because of abuse, manipulation, or ongoing danger.
Forgiveness does not require pretending that evil never happened.
Reconciliation, where possible, involves truth, repentance, and the rebuilding of trust.
But Genesis 33 allows us to witness a remarkable moment of mercy.
The brother Jacob feared embraced him.
And the man who had once grasped his brother's heel now bowed before him.
What a transformation.
Yet even this is not the greatest wonder in the story.
Because Jacob's life was not ultimately about Jacob.
His family was part of a promise that stretched far beyond his lifetime.
Through Jacob, whom God named Israel, came the twelve tribes of Israel.
Through the tribe of Judah came the royal line associated with David.
And in the fullness of God's redemptive plan, Jesus Christ entered human history.
Matthew 1:2 places Jacob directly within the genealogy leading to Christ.
“Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob; and Jacob begat Judas and his brethren.” (KJV)
The Savior's earthly genealogy includes this family.
Not because their sins were admirable.
Not because their dysfunction was holy.
But because God's grace and faithfulness are not dependent on human perfection.
And here we arrive at the heart of the Gospel.
Jesus did not come merely to tell struggling people to try harder.
He came to accomplish what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
He lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
He died on the cross for our sins.
He rose from the dead.
And He calls us to repent and believe in Him.
Jacob's story shows God's faithfulness amid human failure.
Jesus Christ reveals the fullness of God's saving grace.
The apostle Paul later reflected on the story of Jacob and Esau in Romans 9:10–13, emphasizing God's sovereign purpose in election rather than human works.
That passage raises profound theological questions, and faithful Christians have discussed aspects of its interpretation for centuries.
But one truth is unmistakable.
No sinner can purchase God's mercy through personal achievement.
Salvation is not a prize awarded to the morally impressive.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9 (KJV)
The Greek word translated “grace” is χάρις (charis).
In this context, it points to God's undeserved favor in salvation.
Not a reward for the deserving.
Not a payment for religious performance.
Not something earned by giving enough money, attending enough services, or appearing spiritually respectable.
A gift.
Received through faith.
And the next verse reminds us that this grace creates a transformed life.
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works…” — Ephesians 2:10 (KJV)
Good works are not the price of salvation.
They are the fruit of God's saving work.
This is why the Gospel cannot be reduced to a motivational message about overcoming your past.
It is far greater than that.
The Gospel declares that the Son of God entered our broken world to redeem sinners and reconcile them to the Father.
Jesus does not merely improve the image of a damaged life.
He gives new life.
And perhaps that is what someone reading this desperately needs to hear.
You have been trying to fix your reputation when what you truly need is reconciliation with God.
You have been trying to prove that you are no longer the person you once were.
You have been trying to silence guilt through achievement, generosity, or religious activity.
But the deepest problem of the human heart cannot be solved by appearances.
Sin requires forgiveness.
Guilt requires cleansing.
The spiritually dead need life.
And that is precisely why Jesus came.
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners…” — 1 Timothy 1:15 (KJV)
Not people who have successfully hidden their sins.
Not people who have polished their stories until the ugly chapters disappear.
Sinners.
People like Jacob.
People like you.
People like me.
And the grace that saves us does not leave us comfortable in the very sins from which Christ came to deliver us.
It teaches us to turn away from ungodliness and walk in newness of life.
That is repentance.
Not merely feeling embarrassed because we were exposed.
Not simply regretting the consequences of our actions.
But turning toward God with a changed heart, trusting His mercy, and learning to walk in obedience to Jesus Christ.
Maybe your story began with a family conflict you never chose.
Maybe you inherited wounds from people who were supposed to protect you.
Maybe, like Jacob, you have also made choices that wounded others.
Maybe both are true.
But you do not have to make your past your permanent identity.
In Christ, there is forgiveness.
In Christ, there is hope.
In Christ, there is power to begin walking differently.
And no, that does not mean every earthly consequence vanishes overnight.
Jacob still walked with a limp.
Some relationships still require difficult conversations.
Some trust must be rebuilt over time.
Some losses cannot be reversed.
But forgiveness in Christ is not less real because the road to healing remains difficult.
Listen to the promise of 2 Corinthians 5:17:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” (KJV)
The Greek phrase καινὴ κτίσις (kainē ktisis) means “new creation.”
This is not a promise that believers instantly forget their past or become incapable of sin.
It is the declaration that union with Christ brings a new reality—a new life belonging to God's redemptive work.
You are not saved by rewriting your own history.
You are saved by the crucified and risen Christ.
And because of Him, your history no longer has the final word over your standing before God.
Now return, for a moment, to Rebekah.
A woman who waited twenty years.
A woman who finally conceived.
A woman who felt a struggle within her that she could not understand.
A woman who brought her distress to the Lord.
She could not have seen every chapter that would follow.
The rivalry.
The stew.
The deception.
The flight.
The wrestling.
The tears of reunion.
The generations to come.
And certainly, from her immediate perspective, she could not have seen the full unfolding of God's redemptive plan culminating in Jesus Christ.
But God was not improvising a rescue after human failure caught Him by surprise.
His covenant purposes continued through generations of imperfect people.
And that is why this story is so much more than a strange account of twins fighting before birth.
It is a reminder that the Bible tells the truth about humanity.
We are capable of jealousy.
We are capable of betrayal.
We are capable of using even spiritual language to justify selfish desires.
We are capable of hurting people we love.
And yet God is merciful.
Not because sin is harmless.
But because His grace is greater than our ability to save ourselves.
Perhaps you are reading this while carrying a private struggle.
You smile in public, but at home you are exhausted.
You know the right Christian words, but your prayer life has become painfully quiet.
You love Jesus, yet you keep returning to a sin you hate.
You want to forgive someone, but the wound still hurts.
You want to believe that God can use your life, but you keep remembering what you did.
Please hear this carefully.
You do not need to pretend that everything is fine.
Bring the truth into the light.
Confess your sins to God.
Seek wise, trustworthy help where you need it.
Make restitution where appropriate and possible.
Ask forgiveness from those you have harmed.
And place your confidence not in the intensity of your emotions, but in the finished work of Jesus Christ.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9 (KJV)
That promise is not an invitation to casual sin.
It is an invitation to honest repentance and trust in God's faithfulness.
And perhaps today is the day you stop running.
Not because you finally became strong enough to fix yourself.
But because you have finally recognized that Jesus is the Savior you need.
If this story has uncovered something in your heart, I want to invite you to respond—not with a polished religious performance, but with honesty.
You do not have to reveal private details or expose wounds you are not ready to discuss.
Sometimes the first step toward receiving encouragement is simply admitting that you need prayer.
Your experience will not be identical to someone else's, but your words may encourage a person who feels terribly alone.
There is also someone in your life who may need this message.
A brother you have not spoken to in years.
A daughter carrying guilt.
A friend quietly losing hope.
A believer who thinks one terrible decision has permanently disqualified them from God's mercy.
Invite your family, friends, fellow believers, those who have drifted from faith, and even those who are still searching for answers to follow along.
Not because a page can save anyone.
Only Jesus saves.
But because the Word of God deserves to be heard, studied, understood, and lived.
And if this ministry has helped strengthen your faith, there is another meaningful way to participate.
For believers who choose to give as an expression of worship and stewardship, this can be part of their generosity toward Gospel ministry.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
Not the idea that you must pay money to prove that you love God.

Your giving to Gospel Warrior is not automatically the same thing as a biblical tithe to your local church, and it should never replace responsibilities to your household or other commitments you prayerfully believe God has entrusted to you.
It helps sustain the work.
It helps make continued biblical teaching possible.
A single article may be read by someone who has not opened a Bible in years.
A devotional may encourage a struggling believer to return to prayer.
A carefully explained Scripture passage may help someone recognize a misunderstanding they have carried for decades.
We cannot guarantee how many hearts a message will reach or what response each reader will make.
That belongs to God.
But we can faithfully prepare, publish, share, teach, and serve.
These items are not spiritual necessities, and buying them does not make anyone a better Christian.
The library's free resources are there to help you study Scripture, strengthen your understanding, develop a consistent devotional life, and continue growing in faith.
Pray for the ministry.
Invite others to read the Scriptures.
Encourage someone to seek Christ.
Because the mission is never to build a community around a personality.
It is to point people to the Lord Jesus Christ.
And before you leave this story, there is one final image I want you to remember.
Two children struggling in their mother's womb.
A family wounded by favoritism.
A brother running from the consequences of his own deception.
A lonely man sleeping with a stone beneath his head.
A wrestling match in the darkness.
A wounded man walking toward the brother he feared.
And two grown men weeping in an embrace.
What began with a struggle did not end with that struggle.
But even their reunion was not the final destination of the story.
The greater story continued until the promised Savior came.
Jesus Christ.
The One who never deceived.
The One who never sinned.
The One who willingly bore the judgment sinners deserve.
The One who rose victorious from the grave.
The One who calls the guilty to repentance, the weary to come to Him, and the lost to receive eternal life through faith in His name.
That is our hope.
Not that every family story will become beautiful in the way we imagined.
Not that every broken relationship will be restored in this lifetime.
Not that every wound will stop hurting tomorrow.
But that God's saving purpose in Jesus Christ is sure, His grace is sufficient, and His promise of eternal life is greater than anything this broken world can offer.
So if you are still struggling, do not mistake the struggle for the end of your story.
If you have sinned, repent and turn to Christ.
If you have been wounded, seek His help and the support of faithful people who will walk with you in truth and love.
If you are weary, remember that the Savior does not demand that you first make yourself worthy before coming to Him.
Come to Jesus.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come believing that His death and resurrection are sufficient to save.
Because the deepest miracle in this story is not that two brothers eventually embraced.
It is that the God who carried His promise through a broken family would one day send His own Son to redeem broken people.
And that includes people with histories they wish they could erase.
People with regrets they struggle to name.
People who have been fighting battles for so long that they have forgotten what peace feels like.
People like us.
The struggle may have begun before Jacob ever opened his eyes—but it was never greater than the grace of the God who would one day open the way to eternal life through Jesus Christ.
